Background
Marine autonomy has become an increasingly popular topic of discussion over the past decade.
The number of projects and organizations focused on autonomous vessels and supporting
systems has grown substantially across research, defense and commercial sectors. This
represents a trend driven by advances in artificial intelligence, edge computing, and onboard
processing capability. As machine learning algorithms have matured and embedded computing
platforms have become more powerful, energy efficient, and low cost, the technical barriers to
deploying intelligent maritime systems have fallen considerably. Market analyses support this
shift, with the global autonomous shipping market valued at 6.04 billion USD in 2023 and
projected to exceed 13.41 billion USD by 2030. This is primarily driven by continued advances
in sensing, AI-based navigation, and long-endurance vessel design [1].
A major factor behind this rising interest is the inherently dangerous nature of maritime work.
According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, workers in maritime
occupations experience a fatality rate 4.7 times higher than the average American worker, with
commercial fishing and offshore operations consistently ranking among the most hazardous
professions [2]. Reducing the number of personnel required at sea offers a direct pathway to
improving safety while enabling missions that demand long endurance, continuous monitoring,
or operation in remote or high-risk environments.
Despite the momentum behind uncrewed systems, maritime autonomy is still a relatively new
field. Current sensor suites and navigation systems are limited and often require human oversight
or intervention. Radar and optical sensors can be compromised in poor conditions such as heavy
seas, dense fog, or busy coastal environments where weather and wave clutter reduce detection
accuracy. Research efforts such as the European Union's MUNIN project have demonstrated that
autonomous vessels face challenges in sensor fusion, environmental noise rejection, and
algorithmic robustness when operating across dynamic and unpredictable ocean conditions [3].
These limitations underscore the importance of designing vessels that naturally support
predictable behavior, reducing the burden placed on the autonomy stack and increasing the
likelihood of reliable operation with minimal human input.
Hull-form selection plays a central role in addressing these challenges. Trimarans distinguish
themselves from conventional monohulls and catamarans through a three-hull configuration that
distributes buoyancy across a wide beam, significantly reducing rolling and pitching in open
water conditions. Research from the U.S. Naval Surface Warfare Center indicates that trimarans
offer lower hydrodynamic resistance at higher speeds, improved seakeeping performance,
survivability and greater deck area relative to displacement [4]. These characteristics directly

allowing stable operation with minimal corrective control actions.
For these reasons, a trimaran hull was selected over monohull and catamaran alternatives. Its
inherent stability reduces the workload on the autonomy system, while its hydrodynamic
efficiency supports extended uncrewed operation. The multi‑hull configuration also provides a
form of physical redundancy that complements the still‑maturing reliability of autonomous
maritime technologies. Consistent with the goal of minimizing failure points, the vessel uses
differential thrust for steering rather than a mechanically complex rudder system, reducing the
number of electrical and mechanical subsystems that could compromise mission success.

As previously stated, the team decided to pursue a trimaran hull for its advantages over other hull
designs in the case of creating an autonomous vessel with maturing technology. Our design
consists of a large center hull and 2 amas, each connected with 2 40mmx40mm 80/20 aluminum
extrusions on either side. These extrusions are typically made from 6105-T5 alloy, which have
yielding stress of 150MPa, well above necessary tolerance this system will experience in its
intended application. In this connection, the most likely point of failure is the connection
between the hulls and extrusions. To address this issue, 10mm washers were added to the bolts
connecting the 2 parts to spread the force over a larger area, thus reducing stress on that
connection. A CAD model was first created, and it is depicted in the figure 1 below.

Figure 1: Trimaran Hull CAD Model
Following established hull design practices, the average beam-to-length ratio of a trimaran’s
center hull is 1:6 or about 16% the length of the hull. The beam-to-length ratio on this vessel is
325mm/1750mm, which is about ~18.5% the length of the hull, which is fairly close to the 1:6
target. Additionally, the hull has a wave-piercing V-shaped bow profile that slowly transitions
into a flat displacement hull towards the aft.

pages.text:
Propulsion
The propellers are mounted 250 mm below the hull and aft of the hull, supported by
hydrodynamic struts. With the calculated design draft taken into account, the propellers operate
approximately 300 mm below the waterline. Mounting them with this method, as compared to
out the back as done in previous iterations, provides several advantages.
Moving the propeller deeper allows it to operate in undisturbed, clean water inflow and be
unaffected by hull turbulence, resulting in increased energy efficiency and operating range. There
will also be lower cavitation and aeration in rough sea conditions that allows for the propellers to
stay submerged, unlike out the back, where the propeller may not contact the water when heeled.
Additionally, this configuration will create a trimming moment that will lift the hull slightly out
of the water at speed, reducing drag. The moment is given in equation 6, where T is the thrust
and h is the vertical offset of the propeller.

The target motor specs were: 28.8V nominal voltage, a max current of 90A to ensure
compatibility with the existing electrical system, a rated power range between 750W-1500W, and
IP68 rated, as these motors would be operating underwater for extended periods of time. Having
the motors underwater also eliminates the need for a cooling system that requires the added
complexity of pumps and tubing. This power range was selected based on experience with a
Leopard 56110 motor rated at 7560W at last year's competition that strained the electrical system
as its maximum power draw exceeded what the batteries could provide. It was believed that a
65%-80% reduction in rated power was still sufficient to power the boat across 2 motors while
reducing risk. After much consideration, the options for thrusters were narrowed to 3 candidates
that fit the specifications, which are listed in Table 3 below.

Figure 3: Motor Options - Apsiqueen, Flipsky, Hobby Water (Respectively)
The team’s first choice was the Flipsky 56115. However, after weeks of attempting to acquire the
motor and multiple order and payment failures, the team decided to order the APISQUEEN 4190
instead. Unfortunately, the package containing the motors and ESCs was stolen after they were
delivered. The team attempted to source the same motors from a different supplier but could not
find an avenue that fit within the budgetary and time constraints. Finally a pair of DW5490 were
ordered. There were very limited motors in the market that fit the specifications compatible with
the electrical system. Despite being quoted 3-10 days for shipping, there were delays and the
motors were stuck in customs for almost double that time. The DW5490 delivers a combined
rated power of 4000W and 4N*m of torque across 2 motors while fitting into the constraints of
the electrical system to operate safely. Ultimately our team spent about four months trying to
acquire motors.

4 bladed propeller created using Onshape (Figure 4). The propeller was then 3D printed and
coated in epoxy to give it structural rigidity. It is then attached to the motor with
counter-direction blades. The propellers have a diameter of 135mm. With this information, the
necessary torque values can be calculated.
With a goal of finishing the 2 mile course in 10 minutes, the boat has to travel at an average of
12.5mph or ~5.36m/s. At normal cruising speeds, about 50N is needed to move the 42kg vessel.
The required torque needed is calculated by:
𝑇 = 𝐹 * 𝑟 = (50𝑁) * (0. 0575𝑚) = 3. 375𝑁𝑚

(eq. 7)

Based on the calculations, the propulsion system will need to output 3.375Nm to achieve
12.5mph. The selected motors have a combined 4Nm of torque across 2 motors, demonstrating
that the motors are sufficient to reach this desired speed with a total of 8Nm of available max
torque available.

Electrical System
The vehicle is powered by 2 MaxAmps Lithium 8S 20000mAh Li-Ion batteries configured in
parallel. These batteries can deliver a continuous 100 A each; however, running them in parallel
doubles the amperage, allowing us to put more power into our motors. Additionally, these
batteries boast an energy density that is unrivaled by other market options. At 250 Wh/kg, they
outperform almost all other batteries in energy density, especially in the 8S range.

Figure 5: MaxAmps Lithium ion battery
There are a few 6S options with up to 300 Wh/kg, but they are all LiPo batteries which are
significantly less safe than Li-Ion batteries, with a much higher likelihood of combusting if
improperly used. While safer than LiPo batteries to begin with, the MaxAmps Lithium batteries
also have automatic internal cell balancing to prevent an individual cell from getting over
drained and failing before the battery is too low.
The batteries for the craft are stored in the center hull of the boat. They are protected by a marine
grade watertight lid and epoxy to ensure waterproofness in the event of a capsize. Epoxying the

our sensing and controls suite for noise and safety reasons. Our high power safety shutoff is 36V
volt contactor that is controlled by a relay. To power our lower voltage electronics, we use a 14S
rated power conversion module. Using a 14S power module allows the system to safely handle
power spikes like the one we experienced two years ago, which blew our previous 10S rated
power conversion module. The power diagram for the vehicle can be seen below.

pages.text:
Control System

Figure 7: Control and Communications - Signal Diagram
The control system of the craft consists of a Pixhawk 6C flight controller, a common
flight controller for RC drones and aircraft. The flight controller has a built-in IMU. With an
additional GPS and current sensor we are able to monitor key facets of our craft. A Dragonlink
RC two-way radio system is used to transmit telemetry data, such as GPS location, current speed,
and battery voltage and current draw to the user. These components can be used to control the
vessel while it is configured for remote control, however our control architecture also offers
autonomous mode, detailed below.

Autonomous Control
The vessel can be configured for autonomous navigation using QGroundControl software.
QGroundControl is used to create and set a planned path comprised of waypoints and to
configure the radio connection between the RC controller and the flight controller, as well as the
flight controller itself. Then, when the vessel is armed and set to the autonomous mode, it
executes that plan autonomously. The flight controller monitors the data it receives from its
sensors, namely the GPS and accelerometer, and uses S-curve path planning and an L1 controller
that commands an underlying PID network to follow the path outlined by the waypoints, with
Dijkstra’s algorithm for object avoidance. The autonomous navigation does not require an active
connection, radio or otherwise, to the flight controller during operation, only to arm the vessel
and start the plan.

Build & Fabrication
This year, a significant constraint shaped the fabrication approach: the team did not have access
to a CNC machine to mill a foam mold, a desired tool given the increased geometric complexity
of the hull., despite the hull’s increased geometric complexity. To address this, the mold was
produced using FDM 3D printing. The hull was designed in Onshape, chosen for its cloud‑based
collaboration features and accessibility for members with varying engineering backgrounds. The
geometry was divided into smaller, printable sections sized for Bambu X1E and X1 Carbon
printers, with alignment dowels and corresponding holes incorporated to reinforce joints during
assembly. All components were printed in PLA with sparse infill, as the mold would later be
reinforced with fiberglass. The full print process required approximately two weeks and
consumed roughly 10 kg of filament. Once completed, the printed sections were bonded using
super glue to form the complete mold. This process is depicted below.

pages.text:
Figure 11: Fiberglass Veil and Fiberglass Weave Application
A base layer of fiberglass veil was then applied to the mold. A fiberglass veil is a thin,
non‑woven surfacing material composed of randomly oriented fibers bonded into a lightweight
sheet. Its structure allows it to conform easily to complex surfaces, fill micro‑voids, and create a
smooth, uniform base. Veil is commonly used below the waterline to enhance waterproofing and
provide an additional barrier layer, making it an ideal first layer over the PLA mold. After curing
and sanding the veil layer, 6 oz woven fiberglass cloth was applied using West Systems 105B
epoxy with 205B hardener. Woven cloth was selected based on prior experience with
chopped‑strand mat, which proved difficult to work with and produced a rougher finish. During
layup, however, the 6 oz cloth showed limited epoxy absorption and increased air‑bubble
retention due to its density. A lower‑density weave will likely be used in future iterations to
improve conformity and wet‑out. A layer of peel ply was applied to achieve a more uniform
surface. After removal, small craters caused by trapped air were identified and filled with
TotalBoat fairing compound, with curing accelerated using heat, and then sanded smooth.

Figure 12: The Sanding Process

pages.text:
Several challenges emerged throughout the composite layup process, including sharp angles that
trapped air under the mat, as well as the need for precise relief cuts to allow the fiberglass to
conform to complex curvature. These observations will guide refinements in future mold designs
and composite workflows, contributing to a more efficient and repeatable fabrication process.

Electrical Integration
Throughout the hull design process, the mechanical design team collaborated closely with the
electrical and controls team to ensure integrating the electrical system would go smoothly. Holes
in the center hull and amas parallel to the aluminum extrusion were created in the CAD stage to
accommodate wires to the ESCs and motors. The three watertight marine-grade hatches made it
very easy for the electrical team to access the inside of the hull, allowing them to components in
ideal locations, separate high power wires from those carrying essential signals, and integrate the
GPS, battery disconnect switch and antenna externally on the hull.
Industry standard components like xt90 connectors, IP67 rated weatherproof boxes and cable
glands were used to ensure a professional and reliable electronics system.

Risk
When designing Trident, it was important to take into account the risks associated with the
different parts of the craft despite attempting to make the system as simple as possible to reduce
the number of possible failure points. Although there are now 3 hulls, each hull was designed to
be accessible to reach the electrical system. Extensive research and calculations were done to
ensure the electronics were within spec to limit the risk of fires and other potential hazards
related to overloaded electrical systems.
Care and proper precautions are taken when working with the batteries that provide
power to the vehicle. The boat operates on Lithium ion batteries, which are safer than
LiPo batteries, but still pose risks. When the batteries are not in use, they are stored in a
flammables bag or in a flammables cabinet, and it is ensured that they are
charged properly to avoid damaging the batteries and increasing their risk of harm. There
is also always sand available in our lab space, in case a fire were to occur.
The team worked extensively with fiberglass and epoxy this year. Fabricating the hull with these
materials exposes team members to harmful chemicals, especially during layups, sanding, and
cutting of fiberglass. Additional hazards included exposure to toxic fumes from the fuming
compound and from sanding the PLA material. To minimize the risk when working with these
materials, it is ensured that proper protective equipment, including gloves, masks, goggles, and
respirators are worn. It is also verified with instruction manuals that these materials are utilized
correctly and safely.

Figure 14: Contactor Kill Switch

To account for any risks that could occur during the race, the craft has a contactor kill switch
installed, in addition to a physical kill switch, that allows ---- to be shut
down remotely or automatically if the GPS signal is lost. That means if any issue is to occur
during the race, the vehicle will quickly and safely shut down to minimize any potential hazards.

Conclusion
Trident is the result of well over 1000 hours of work from the dedicated team at NUWave. It
boasts a wide variety of safety features from contactors to waterproof hatches to create a secure
craft. Its goal is to bring new innovations to the Promoting Electric Propulsion Competition in
line with 6 new innovative classes such as the autonomous class this year. The boat aims to
differentiate itself from the usual monohulls and catamarans often seen at the competition. With
this boat, NUWave demonstrates its underlying commitment to continuous improvement year
after year as well as the importance of making robotics accessible to everyone, no matter their
skill level. From the first wooden, square hull NUWave entered into this competition over 2
years ago, to experimenting with fabricating with fiberglass and constructing a powertrain from
the ground up last year, to now fabricating with advanced fiberglassing techniques on a much
more complex hull and exploring new innovative designs. T, the team has come a long way and
looks to improve even more in the future. The team would like to give a special thanks to the
people over at InRiver Tank and Boat for their support and guidance, and look forward to
fostering this partnership for the foreseeable future and upcoming projects.
When considering future directions, the team is looking into the feasibility of
constructing a hydrofoiling vessel as we hone our skills and look to enter the competition with
more innovative products and bring a new era to PEP.
